<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Differentially private (DP) synthetic data generation plays a pivotal role in developing large language models (LLMs) on private data, where data owners cannot provide eyes-on access to individual examples.
Generating DP synthetic data typically involves a difficult trade-off. On one hand, DP finetuning methods train an LLM as a synthetic data generator with formal privacy guarantees, yet it still requires the raw content of private examples for model training. However, methods that avoid direct exposure to private data are bounded by an off-the-shelf, un-finetuned model, whose outputs often lack domain fidelity.
<span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Can we <span id="abstract1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">train</span> an LLM to generate high-quality synthetic text without eyes-on access to individual private examples? </span>
In this work, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning</span> (DP-RFT), an online reinforcement learning algorithm for synthetic data generation with LLMs. DP-RFT leverages DP-protected nearest-neighbor votes from an eyes-off private corpus as a reward signal for on-policy synthetic samples generated by an LLM. The LLM iteratively learns to generate synthetic data to maximize the expected DP votes through Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). We evaluate DP-RFT for long-form and domain-specific synthetic data generation, such as news articles, meeting transcripts, and medical article abstracts.
Our experiments show that DP-RFT closes the gap between private evolution and DP finetuning methods in terms of the fidelity and downstream utility of the generated synthetic data, while respecting the private data boundary.</p>
  
</div>
<div class="ltx_keywords">
<h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_keywords">Keywords: </h6>Machine Learning, ICML
</div><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_affiliationnotice"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">affiliationnotice: </span>*Work done during an internship at Microsoft.</span></span></span>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in their capabilities through massive-scale training <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kaplan et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Biderman et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
However, LLM training requires centralized access to its training data. This is typically incompatible with <span id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">private data</span>, where data owners cannot provide eyes-on access to the data due to privacy constraints, regulations, or other reasons <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlini et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Panda et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Differentially-private</span> (DP) synthetic data has emerged as a responsible way of circumventing the need for eyes-on data access. The goal is to leverage LLMs to generate a synthetic dataset that is statistically similar to the private dataset <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jordon et al., 2018</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Harder et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, while ensuring the privacy guarantee that individual samples in the original data cannot be inferred from the model outputs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dwork et al., 2006</a>)</cite>. DP synthetic data can be used for downstream model development
with intact privacy guarantee thanks to DP’s post-processing properties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dwork et al., 2014</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Existing DP synthetic data generation methods typically face a difficult trade-off between data quality versus the required level of access to private dataset during data generation.
While DP finetuning methods, e.g. DP-SGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi et al., 2016</a>)</cite>, provide privacy guarantee when training the synthetic data generator on the private dataset, they still require data custodians to share and expose raw private data samples in the training process <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ponomareva et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
On the other hand,
methods which avoid direct exposure to private data e.g. Aug-PE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, leverage iterative prompting to guide off-the-shelf LLMs to generate data that are more similar to the private distribution. However, as such approaches are bounded by samples generated from a frozen LLM, the outputs often lack domain fidelity.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To get the best of both worlds, we propose <em id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning</em> (DP-RFT), a reinforcement learning (RL) algorithm for training LLMs as DP synthetic data generators without the need to expose individual private examples to LLM during the process. Building upon the reward-based RL post-training techniques for LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zelikman et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jaech et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Guo et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, DP-RFT leverages DP-protected nearest-neighbor votes (DP Votes, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al. (2024)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. (2024)</a></cite>) from an eyes-off private corpus as a reward signal for LLM’s on-policy synthetic sample generation. The DP-votes can be calculated within the boundary of the private data and then exposed to LLM with formal privacy guarantee, so that the private data owners do not need to provide access for individual private examples to LLM during training. The LLM learns from reward feedback to generate synthetic data to maximize the expected DP votes through Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al.</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">2017</a></cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate DP-RFT for <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">long-form</span> synthetic data generation with different domains and types of text, such as news articles <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Narayan et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, meeting transcripts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2021</a>)</cite>, LLM-user chat logs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and medical article abstracts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. We train DP-RFT models under different levels of privacy budget, and evaluate the generated synthetic data by intrinsic quality (§ <a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Similarity evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>), as well as downstream utility when the synthetic data is used as training data for another language model (§ <a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Downstream evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>).
Our experiments show that DP-RFT outperforms Aug-PE in terms of the fidelity and downstream utility of the generated synthetic data, and closes the gap between DP finetuning and Aug-PE in terms of downstream utility. Our key contributions are:</p>
<ol id="S1.I1" class="ltx_enumerate ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">New finetuning method for DP synthetic data generation</em>: We propose DP-RFT , which leverages DP-protected reward function and reinforcement learning to train a LLM against private corpus, without <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">ever</span> ingesting private examples directly during the training process and hence satisfying the <span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">eyes-off</span> constraint.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">In-depth experiments and analyses</em>: We conduct comprehensive evaluation of our methods on four datasets, showing significant improvement on downstream utility, especially for a tight privacy budget and on dataset which are out-of-distribution for the backbone language model. Our qualitative analysis further reveals that  DP-RFT is able to better capture lexical and structural similarity of long-form, structural outputs.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2602.18633v1/dp-rft-fig-1-new.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:354/168;" width="354" height="168" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">An illustration of DP-RFT and comparison with prior methods. DP-RFT fine-tunes a language model (LM) to generate texts similar to the private document with reinforcement learning, guided by a DP-protected nearest-neighbor votes as reward. Unlike DP-Finetuning which requires accessing the private data directly, DP-RFT and  Aug-PE allow downstream model training outside of the private boundary. While  Aug-PE is bounded by samples generated from a frozen LM,  DP-RFT generates synthetic data with higher fidelity by training an LM to generate texts more similar to the private data.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Background and Related work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Differential Privacy with LLMs.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As LLMs are increasingly deployed in many real-world cases, preserving the privacy of training and evaluation data has been an active research area. One popular approach is to apply DP-SGD  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi et al., 2016</a>)</cite> to train LLMs for classification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>)</cite> or generation tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mattern et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kurakin et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ngong et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tan et al., 2025</a>)</cite>. Later work proposed training-free approaches, such as injecting calibrated DP noise into the token-by-token generation process of LLMs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Tang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Flemings et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Duan et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, or aggregating multiple LLM outputs in a DP manner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
While these methods provide theoretical DP guarantees, they all require exposing the private data as input to the LLM. In practice, there could be regulatory constraints that require the private data to be completely <span id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">eyes-off</span>, preventing the adoption of such methods. Private Evolution (PE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>)</cite> is a newly emerged framework to address this challenge.
It proposes an iterative prompting pipeline which steers the model generation to be more similar to the private data, as measured by embedding similarity.
While these methods avoid private inputs, their reliance on un-finetuned models limits the synthetic data quality. Our DP-RFT aims to take the best of both worlds: adapting model weights to better fit private data without directly inputting it into the model. Recent work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Nguyen et al., 2025</a>)</cite> proposes to generate synthetic data via gradient matching, which requires gradient computation on private data. Notably, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hou et al. (2025)</a></cite> recently proposed fine-tuning LLMs using embedding similarity as a reward with an offline reinforcement learning algorithm (DPO; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Rafailov et al.</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">2023</a></cite>).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) for LLMs.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We briefly review how reinforcement learning is used to post-train large language models. Let a language model with parameters <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> define a policy <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> over token sequences given a prompt <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. The goal of RFT is to update <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> so that samples <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="d\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>∼</mo><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0.167em">∣</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid p)</annotation></semantics></math> have higher task-specific utility, quantified by a scalar reward <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R(d,p)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R(d,p)</annotation></semantics></math>. In modern LLM post-training, <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> can come from a learned reward model (e.g., RLHF, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ouyang et al.</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">2022</a></cite>), or from verifiable signals (e.g., passing tests in code/math), and training proceeds by maximizing the cumulative rewards. Practically, RFT alternates between: (i) sampling on-policy generations from <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pi_{\theta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>π</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pi_{\theta}</annotation></semantics></math> for a batch of prompts; (ii) computing scalar rewards for each sample; and (iii) updating <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\theta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>θ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\theta</annotation></semantics></math> via a policy gradient method (e.g., PPO, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al.</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">2017</a></cite>; or GRPO, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shao et al.</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">2024</a></cite>) on those samples. Compared to supervised fine-tuning (SFT), where LLM ingests reference texts as input during training, RFT directly optimizes the task metric exposed by <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> and is thus effective when high-quality labels are scarce or when a reward function <math id="S2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math> can be defined. The fact that RFT does not ingest example outputs during training is the key to our DP-RFT algorithm’s design.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a set of private documents <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">priv</sub>, our goal is to train a language model <math id="S3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> that generates synthetic documents <math id="S3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub">syn</sub> similar to <math id="S3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>D</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_sub">priv</sub>. <math id="S3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> takes an input prompt <span id="S3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span> which contains public information about the private corpus and produces a synthetic document <math id="S3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>. We describe our method, DP-RFT, which leverages reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT) to train <math id="S3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> against a DP-protected reward function <math id="S3.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>R</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R</annotation></semantics></math>. We illustrate the workflow of  DP-RFT, as well as its differences from prior approaches, including DP-Finetuning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Abadi et al., 2016</a>)</cite> and Augmented Private Evolution (Aug-PE; <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeyear"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">2024</a></cite>) in <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Generating input prompts</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use a large language model (LLM) to construct input prompts which contain public information about the target domain.
We construct a diverse set of prompts to encourage diverse generation from <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> following Augmented Private Evolution (Aug-PE) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> for training and inference of DP-RFT. We focus on one or both of the two axes of diversity (1) content diversity and (2) length diversity. For content diversity, we generate a set of keywords using an LLM. For instance, for BBC articles, we prompt an LLM to generate a list of topics (e.g. Politics, Sports), along with keywords associated with each topic. We obtain a set of prompts, each with a different set of keywords, which we use as input to <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math>. For length diversity, we define a possible range of length for the private documents and random sample one length to include in the prompt (e.g. “The generated document should contain around 300 words”). We include the details of the procedure in §<a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation details of DP-RFT ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Rewards</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">DP voting as reward.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aug-PE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> prompts language models to generate multiple synthetic documents and iteratively generate synthetic documents via a process called <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DP voting</span>: each private document votes for a synthetic document that is most similar to them measured with a similarity function, such as a text embedding model. They find that selecting synthetic documents that receive more votes (i.e. close to more private documents in the embedding space) lead to better synthetic documents and hence downstream performance.
We take inspiration from Aug-PE and propose the following new designs to the DP-voting mechanism and the iterative generation-sampling process:
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Using raw similarity scores as votes.</span> In Aug-PE, each private sample votes only for its closest synthetic document, producing a binary (1 or 0) signal. This discards valuable information in the raw similarity scores, such as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how much</span> one synthetic sample is better than another. To capture this richer signal, we instead use the raw similarity scores <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sim(d,D_{priv,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sim(d,D_{priv,i})</annotation></semantics></math> directly as votes from the <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math>-th private document <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="D_{priv,i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">D_{priv,i}</annotation></semantics></math> to the synthetic document <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, where <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sim</annotation></semantics></math> is a similarity measure (e.g. text embedding similarity).
<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) DP-RFT.</span>
While Aug-PE can promote synthetic documents that are similar to the private documents, the model is untrained, and hence has limited steerability. We instead leverage the votes as the reward in Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) to steer <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> to generate synthetic documents more similar to the private corpus. Concretely, for a synthetic document <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> and a predefined similarity measure <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sim</annotation></semantics></math>, we define <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}=\frac{1}{{|D_{priv}|}}\sum_{i=1}^{i=|D_{priv}|}sim(d,D_{priv,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><msubsup><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mrow></msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}=\frac{1}{{|D_{priv}|}}\sum_{i=1}^{i=|D_{priv}|}sim(d,D_{priv,i})</annotation></semantics></math> as the reward.</p>
</div>

                <span id="algx1.l16.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="algx1.l16.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">end</span><span id="algx1.l16.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;"> </span><span id="algx1.l16.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">forReturn</span><span id="algx1.l16.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">: </span><math id="algx1.l16.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathsize="0.900em">R</mi><mrow><mi mathsize="0.900em">s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi mathsize="0.900em">m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="algx1.l16.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
</span>
</div>
</div>
</div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F2.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 2</span>: </span><span id="S3.F2.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Procedure for computing similarity reward (<math id="S3.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>) given a noise multiplier <math id="S3.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> for a batch of <math id="S3.F2.m15" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math> synthetic samples.</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ensuring differential privacy.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To ensure differential privacy, we add Gaussian noise to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> following Aug-PE. For a synthetic example <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, we first obtain its similarity to each of the private documents <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sim(d,D_{priv,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sim(d,D_{priv,i})</annotation></semantics></math> and clip the similarity score to a threshold <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>. Given a noise multiplier <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> and a batch of synthetic samples of size <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>, we add Gaussian noise <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma c\sqrt{s})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma c\sqrt{s})</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sum_{i}sim(d,D_{priv,i})" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mi>i</mi></msub><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>v</mi></mrow><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sum_{i}sim(d,D_{priv,i})</annotation></semantics></math>, i.e., the sum of similarity between the synthetic document and all private documents. Finally, we obtain the average similarity scores across all private documents. We provide the pseudocode of this procedure in <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ DP voting as reward. ‣ 3.2 Rewards ‣ 3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 2</span></a>.
The privacy analysis follows the Private Evolution framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which is reproduced in §<a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a> for completeness.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Mitigating reward hacking.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Although optimizing for <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> can lead to synthetic documents similar to the private corpus defined by <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="sim" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">sim</annotation></semantics></math>, relying only on <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> as the sole reward can lead to reward hacking <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Amodei et al., 2016</a>; <a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pan et al., 2022</a>)</cite>. Unlike prior RFT methods which focus on math and coding problems <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">DeepSeek-AI, 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2025</a>)</cite> where a verifiable reward (e.g. presence of the gold answer string) can be defined, generating documents that are similar to a set of documents is relatively open-ended and unconstrained. Moreover, text embedding models are known to have various biases <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Coelho et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fayyaz et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and could assign high similarity scores to dissimilar documents, especially when embedding <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">long</span> documents. Thus, in addition to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>, we employ a reward <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> that measures adherence to the input prompt to prevent reward hacking.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              While RL algorithms such as PPO includes a KL penalty term to reduce divergence from the reference model, we find that increasing KL penalty does not resolve the issue in our preliminary experiments. Instead, it discourages the model from learning to generate samples closer to the private distribution.</span></span></span> We implement <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> as a combination of LLM-as-a-judge and rule-based checks (§<a href="#S4" title="4 Experiments ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To combine the two rewards, we use a threshold approach. We set the reward to 0 if <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> is less than a threshold <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> and otherwise return <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>. The final reward is defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R=\begin{cases}R_{\text{sim}}&amp;\text{if }R_{\text{prompt}}&gt;\tau\\
0&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mrow><mrow><mtext>if </mtext><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>prompt</mtext></msub></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mi>τ</mi></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mn>0</mn></mtd><mtd class="ltx_align_left" columnalign="left"><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R=\begin{cases}R_{\text{sim}}&amp;\text{if }R_{\text{prompt}}&gt;\tau\\
0&amp;\text{otherwise}\end{cases}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We train DP-RFT  using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Schulman et al. (2017)</a></cite>).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Evaluation settings</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate DP-RFT and the baselines on four publicly available datasets that are treated as private datasets, covering different domains and document structures:</p>
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Domain-specific document-level data:</em> <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PubMed</span>, which contains abstracts of medical papers crawled by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al. (2023)</a></cite> from 2023/08/01 to 2023/08/07; <span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">BBC News article</span> from 2010 to 2017 released by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Narayan et al. (2018)</a></cite></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><em id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Structured long-form data:</em> <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">WildChat</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which contains chat history between a user and an LLM; collected between 2023 to 2024 and <span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QMSum</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhong et al., 2021</a>)</cite> which contains meeting transcripts.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The average number of tokens for PubMed, BBC article, WildChat and QMSum are <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="361" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>361</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">361</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="513" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>513</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">513</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{,}799" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,799</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}799</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2{,}857" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>2,857</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2{,}857</annotation></semantics></math> respectively. We include details about these datasets in §<a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix E Experiment details ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a> in the appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Intrinsic evaluation: similarity with real data.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report quantitative metrics including the average and maximal embedding similarity with the private corpus and the embedding distribution distance, i.e., the Fréchet Inception Distance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Heusel et al., 2017</a>)</cite>, following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. As it is non-trivial to measure similarity of long documents, we also employ LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate pairwise similarity of two synthetic documents against a private document and conduct qualitative evaluation on document structure in §<a href="#S6" title="6 Analysis and ablation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Extrinsic evaluation: downstream performance.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Aside from intrinsic similarity evaluation, the synthetic text should be helpful in downstream utility. We fine-tune a language model via next token prediction on the synthetic text generated and report the next token prediction accuracy on the private test set. Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hou et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, we conduct experiments fine-tuning BERT<sub id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Devlin et al., 2019</a>)</cite> as a causal language model by modifying bidirectional attention to causal attention. As BERT<sub id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub> is relatively small-scale, we also fine-tune and evaluate GPT-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Radford et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>DP-RFT and baseline settings</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide the implementation details for each component for DP-RFT  as described in §<a href="#S3" title="3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>: For all datasets, we use Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qwen Team, 2024</a>)</cite> as <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math><sub id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_sub">gen</sub> and gte-Qwen-2-1.5B-Instruct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite> to measure <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>. For WildChat and QMSum, we also measure the distributions of word-level jaccard similarity and word counts of all speech turn in a synthetic vs. private example, and use their KL divergence as two additional terms in <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>, in order to encourage <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math> to learn the structural properties of private corpus.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><math id="S4.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math>: We use gpt-4o <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2024</a>)</cite> as the LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate how well the output adheres to the prompt. Concretely, given the input prompt <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math> and generated documents <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math>, the model outputs a scalar rating from 1 to 10 on how well <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> adheres to <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>p</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p</annotation></semantics></math>. We include the exact prompt in §<a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation details of DP-RFT ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>. To evaluate adherence to the length instruction for the BBC article and PubMed, we employ a rule-based approach that checks the difference between the length of the generated documents and the specified length in the prompt. If the length difference is greater than a threshold <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> or the LLM-as-a-judge output is less than a threshold <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math>, we set the reward to 0. We set the threshold <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tau" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>τ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tau</annotation></semantics></math> to 6 and <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>d</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d</annotation></semantics></math> as {50, 100} for PubMed and BBC articles respectively. We conduct ablation studies on removing <math id="S4.SS2.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{p}rompt" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{p}rompt</annotation></semantics></math> in § <a href="#S6.SS2" title="6.2 Ablation study ‣ 6 Analysis and ablation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Input prompts.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we construct input prompts for each dataset by prompting an LM to generate keywords based on public knowledge. We design a multi-stage pipeline to ensure diversity of the prompts. For BBC articles, we first prompt the language model to generate a list of category of BBC articles. We then prompt the models to generate keywords for each categories. For PubMed, we use the writers released by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and prompt the language model to generate 100 technical terms for each of the writer. The prompt template for each dataset in <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We consider several baseline methods which trains an LM with differential privacy. <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Aug-PE</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, which steers generation from a language model to be more similar to the private data by iterative prompting; <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">QWEN</span>: which prompts the backbone model to generate synthetic data; this represents the performance of the model before DP-RFT training. We also compared to <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DP-FT</span> which fine-tunes the model on the downstream task with DP-SGD <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yu et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2022</a>)</cite>, though we note that <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">DP-FT</span> requires ingesting the private text as <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">input</span> to train the model, and thus violating the <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">eyes-off</span> setting. For all datasets, we follow the setup of <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al. (2024)</a></cite> and report Aug-PE results of 10 iterations. We use the same generation model and embedding model as DP-RFT to ensure a fair comparison. We use the input prompt for DP-RFT as <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RANDOM_API</span> and the fill-in-the-blank <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VARIATION_API</span>. We include exact prompts in §<a href="#A5.SS1.SSS1" title="E.1.1 Baseline details ‣ E.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix E Experiment details ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.1</span></a> in the Appendix; as well as example private text and generated text in §<a href="#A8.SS1" title="H.1 Example text ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H.1</span></a>. We report results for training on a subset of private data (2,000) and compare with training on 2,000 data generated by  DP-RFT and  Aug-PE, except for QMSum, which only contains 700 examples in total. We generate synthetic text and keep the training data size consistent for all methods.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Privacy Setting.</h5>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the performance of different privacy budgets controlled by <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>. We train for 100 steps for PubMed and QMSum, and 200 steps for BBC articles and WildChat. We experiment with privacy budgets <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math> = {1,2,4,<math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\infty</annotation></semantics></math>}. The Gaussian noise multipliers being added to the DP votes are derived by the number of training steps and the size of the private corpus accordingly. The details are described in § <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>. For DP-RFT, we use noise multiplier <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> = {41.90, 22.14, 11.86, 0} for PubMed, <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> = {29.98, 16.45, 9.17, 0} for QMSum, and <math id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math> = {52.50, 28.07, 15.23, 0} for BBC articles and WildChat. We clip the maximum value of raw similarity score at 0.5 for BBC article and PubMed, and 0.8 for QMSum and WildChat.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Results</h2>

<td id="S5.T1.11.3.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t"><span id="S5.T1.11.3.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;--ltx-bg-color:#D9D9D9;">42.33</span></td>

<section id="S5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.1 </span>Downstream evaluation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 1</span></a>reports the results on downstream performance for GPT-2 and BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">DP-RFT outperforms Aug-PE across datasets and privacy budgets.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Across all datasets and privacy budgets, DP-RFT consistently achieves higher downstream accuracy than Aug-PE on both GPT-2 and BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub>. The gains are particularly pronounced for BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub>, with up to 22%, 35%, 2%, and 47% relative improvement on PubMed, BBC, WildChat, and QMSum, respectively, and are also substantial for GPT-2, reaching up to 10%, 4%, 4%, and 2% on these datasets. These improvements indicate that DP-RFT is able to effectively shift the distribution of the LLM compared to Aug-PE, which iteratively prompts a frozen LLM. In addition, DP-RFT consistently outperforms the un-finetuned QWEN baseline (except for BBC at <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=2" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=2</annotation></semantics></math>, where performance is comparable), further demonstrating the benefits of training <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\text{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\text{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">DP-RFT outperforms DP-FT under tight privacy budgets and low-data regimes for BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.1" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub>.</h5>

<div id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While DP-FT operates under a looser privacy constraint (i.e., violating the <span id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">eyes-off</span> setting), its performance for BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub> degrades substantially as the privacy budget decreases, underperforming DP-RFT across all datasets when <math id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\neq\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\neq\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. In contrast, for GPT-2, DP-FT consistently outperforms DP-RFT across privacy budgets and datasets. We attribute this difference to the fact that BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub> is converted into a causal language model during fine-tuning, which differs from its pre-training setup. To further investigate this effect, we scale up the amount of private data to the full dataset in §<a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Downstream evaluation with BERTsmall ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>, observing improved downstream performance for DP-FT. Yet, DP-RFT continues to outperform DP-FT for BERT<sub id="S5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub> in low-data regimes (e.g., QMSum with only 700 examples) or under tight privacy budgets, highlighting its practical advantages in realistic privacy-constrained settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">5.2 </span>Similarity evaluation</h3>

<div id="S5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><a href="#S5.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 5.2 Similarity evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 2</span></a>reports similarity metrics between synthetic and private data. Overall, DP-RFT exhibits higher similarity to private documents than the unfine-tuned QWEN across both instance-level metrics (mean and maximum similarity) and distributional measures (FID), indicating that DP-RFT more effectively captures the underlying data distribution. In addition, DP-RFT outperforms Aug-PE for instance-level metrics in most settings, with the advantage becoming more pronounced under tighter privacy budgets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We observe dataset-dependent trends in similarity performance. For example, with <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, DP-RFT and Aug-PE achieve comparable embedding similarity on PubMed, whereas DP-RFT yields approximately 20% higher similarity on the other three datasets. We attribute this difference to PubMed being closer to the distribution of the backbone generator <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\text{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\text{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math>, making it easier to steer via prompting. To quantify this, we measure the distance between the target distribution and <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\text{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\text{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math> using perplexity of the private data under <math id="S5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{\text{gen}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mtext>gen</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{\text{gen}}</annotation></semantics></math>, finding that PubMed has lower perplexity (6.75) than BBC (9.11) and QMSum (10.14). Although WildChat also exhibits low perplexity (4.04) as it contains model-generated texts, its long-form and structured nature makes it more difficult to steer through iterative prompting. We note that Aug-PE achieves lower FiD on PubMed and WildChat, which may be attributed to the fact that Aug-PE explicitly optimizes FiD and can therefore perform better on distributions that are more familiar to the base model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To complement embedding similarity, we conduct an LLM-as-a-judge pairwise similarity evaluation against private document on use of word and tone, finding that  DP-RFT is consistently preferred over  Aug-PE across all datasets. We describe the setting and results in details in §<a href="#A8" title="Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>

DP-RFT generates documents that are more similar to the private dataset than baseline methods as measured by embedding similarity.</span></figcaption>

<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Analysis and ablation</h2>

<figure id="S6.F3" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S6.F3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 3</span>: </span><span id="S6.F3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">

Real (private) WildChat examples are shown in gray.
</span></figcaption>
