<section id="S6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.1 </span>Qualitative Analysis on the Synthetic Examples</h3>

<div id="S6.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the effect of DP-RFT training and the properties the generated synthetic data, we analyze the distributional similarity between synthetic vs. real on private WildChat conversations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Lexical Similarity.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the distribution of Jaccard similarity between each synthetic example and its <span id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">most</span> similar private example, as shown in <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 6 Analysis and ablation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a>. Across privacy budgets, examples generated by DP-RFT exhibit higher lexical overlap with the private data than those produced by Aug-PE. In contrast, the distribution of examples from Aug-PE is more spread out, potentially indicating that Aug-PE outputs are more diverse, despite lower fidelity in terms of lexical similarity. This observation is consistent with the FiD results in §<a href="#S5.SS2" title="5.2 Similarity evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.2</span></a>, where Aug-PE achieves lower FiD despite worse average embedding similarity. Incorporating more explicit diversity control into DP-RFT is a promising direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Structural Similarity.</h5>

<div id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For structured data, both content and structural similarity of synthetic examples are important. <a href="#S6.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 6 Analysis and ablation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 3</span></a> compares the per-turn word-count distributions of synthetic and real WildChat conversations across privacy budgets. Overall, synthetic data generated by DP-RFT more closely matches the private distribution than Aug-PE across all privacy settings. Interestingly, however, Aug-PE better captures the bi-modal structure of the distribution, reflecting the mixture of short user turns and longer assistant responses. One possible explanation is that Aug-PE employs a generate-then-select strategy over a large candidate set at each iteration <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, whereas DP-RFT optimizes over smaller mini-batches of rollouts. Future work can examine the effect of rollout batch size in DP-RFT training more closely.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.2 </span>Ablation study</h3>

<div id="S6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose to include <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> to mitigate reward hacking by over-optimizing on <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> (§<a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Rewards ‣ 3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a>). We conduct ablation study which removes <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> from the reward on PubMed with <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\infty</annotation></semantics></math> and report evaluation on both downstream performance and similarity measure. Results are reported in <a href="#S6.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 6.2 Ablation study ‣ 6 Analysis and ablation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 3</span></a>. We see that while model trained without <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> (using <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> as the reward) achieves higher embedding similarity with the private corpus, the downstream performance is notably worse across the two models. This suggests that solely optimizing for embedding similarity could harm performance. We further conduct ablation study on varying <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S6.SS2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math> in §<a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Ablation study ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S6.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S6.T3.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 3</span>: </span><span id="S6.T3.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Ablating <math id="S6.T3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> for QMSum when <math id="S6.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>. Removing <math id="S6.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> leads to better embedding similarity but results in worse downstream performance.</span></figcaption>

</section>
<section id="S6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">6.3 </span>Computational Overhead.</h3>

<div id="S6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Computational cost is an important consideration for practical deployment of synthetic data generation methods. We benchmark the wall-clock GPU hours required by DP-RFT and Aug-PE under our WildChat experimental setting. DP-RFT consists of two phases: <span id="S6.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(1) Training</span>, where 200 optimization steps require approximately 5 hours on 8 A100 GPUs (40 GPU hours total), and <span id="S6.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(2) Inference</span>, where generating 2,000 samples requires roughly 1 A100 GPU hour using vLLM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kwon et al., 2023</a>)</cite>. In contrast, Aug-PE does not involve model training but incurs substantial cost during iterative generation: producing 2,000 samples per iteration requires approximately 10 GPU hours, resulting in a total of 100 GPU hours over 10 iterations<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">2</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            We use the official implementation at <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA</a>.</span></span></span>. While Aug-PE avoids a training phase, its iterative procedure is computationally expensive, particularly for long-form text generation. In comparison, the training cost of DP-RFT is a one-time expense, after which synthetic data can be generated efficiently.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S7" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">7 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce DP-RFT, a reinforcement learning method for training language models to generate synthetic data aligned with a private corpus <span id="S7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without</span> ingesting individual private examples. The key idea of our method is to steer the model with reinforcement learning guided by a similarity measure with the private document as reward, while respecting the eyes-off constraint. Through extensive experiments on four datasets spanning diverse domains and structures, we show that DP-RFT consistently improves both fidelity and downstream utility over prior eyes-off baselines such as Aug-PE, and narrows the gap with DP finetuning methods under tight privacy budgets.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Impact Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This work advances machine learning by exploring a reinforcement learning–based approach to differentially private synthetic data generation without eyes-on access to private examples. By using DP-protected similarity signals as training feedback,  DP-RFT enables large language models to generate synthetic texts better aligned with private data distributions while respecting formal privacy constraints. This reduces the need for direct exposure to sensitive data and may help lower privacy risks in applications where data sharing is restricted. More broadly, our results suggest a path toward more practical and responsible use of LLMs in privacy-sensitive domains.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Large Language Model Usage</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use services powered by large language models (through ChatGPT and Grammarly) to fix grammatical errors and polish the writing in this submission. We do not use LLM-aid for other aspects of the paper writing.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Reproducibility statement</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We include implementation details for reproducing  DP-RFT in Section <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Implementation details of DP-RFT ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a> and for reproducing baseline methods in Section <a href="#A5.SS1.SSS1" title="E.1.1 Baseline details ‣ E.1 Datasets ‣ Appendix E Experiment details ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1.1</span></a>. Implementation details for downstream evaluation is documented at <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Downstream evaluation with BERTsmall ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Implementation details of DP-RFT</h2>

<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We train both the actor and critic models using PPO algorithm on a single node with 8 A100 GPUs. We set the batch size to 128, with two samples per 64 samples each. We set the max completion tokens to 512, 1024, 2,048 and 2,048 for PubMed abstract, BBC article, QMSum and WildChat respectively. We train the model with the <span id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">veRL</span> library.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Input prompts</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For BBC articles, we sample length from a Gaussian distribution with mean of 400 words and standard deviation of 100 words within the range of [100, 900] words (inclusive). We round the number of words to the closest 100. For PubMed, we sample uniformly from [100, 400] words and round the number to the closest 50. We include the example input prompt for each dataset in <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>. We include prompt used to construct the keywords in the input prompt in <a href="#A4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Reward model</h5>

<div id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We include the prompt used for obtaining <math id="A3.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{prompt}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{prompt}</annotation></semantics></math> in Table <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Privacy Analysis</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The privacy analysis of DP-RFT follows the Private Evolution framework <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lin et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, with modifications only in the sensitivity analysis of the mechanism.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Firstly, we analyze the privacy cost of the procedure in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ DP voting as reward. ‣ 3.2 Rewards ‣ 3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Each private sample contributes a vector of size <math id="A4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>s</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s</annotation></semantics></math>. By the clipping operation, each entry of the vector has absolute value at most <math id="A4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>c</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c</annotation></semantics></math>, so its <math id="A4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm is bounded by <math id="A4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\sqrt{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\sqrt{s}</annotation></semantics></math>. Consequently, adding or removing a single private sample changes <math id="A4.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{sim}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{sim}}</annotation></semantics></math> by at most <math id="A4.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="c\sqrt{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">c\sqrt{s}</annotation></semantics></math> in <math id="A4.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> norm. Adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise with standard deviation <math id="A4.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma c\sqrt{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma c\sqrt{s}</annotation></semantics></math> then corresponds to the standard Gaussian mechanism <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dwork et al., 2014</a>)</cite> with noise multiplier <math id="A4.p2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>σ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The overall DP-RFT algorithm performs <math id="A4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> iterations of Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ DP voting as reward. ‣ 3.2 Rewards ‣ 3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, which can be viewed as <math id="A4.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math> adaptive compositions of the Gaussian mechanism. By Corollary 3.3 in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dong et al. (2022)</a></cite>,<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          See the arXiv version: <a href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02383" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.02383</a>.</span></span></span> this is equivalent to a single Gaussian mechanism with effective noise multiplier <math id="A4.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma/\sqrt{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mi>T</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma/\sqrt{T}</annotation></semantics></math>. Therefore, we can apply the tight bounds for Gaussian mechanisms from <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Balle and Wang (2018)</a></cite> to analyze the privacy cost. In particular, given any two of <math id="A4.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="A4.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\delta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>δ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\delta</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="A4.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma/\sqrt{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mi>T</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma/\sqrt{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, their analysis allows us to solve for the third. For example, for a target privacy budget <math id="A4.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\epsilon,\delta)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>δ</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\epsilon,\delta)</annotation></semantics></math>, one can compute the required noise multiplier <math id="A4.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma/\sqrt{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo>/</mo><msqrt><mi>T</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma/\sqrt{T}</annotation></semantics></math>, which in turn specifies the amount of noise <math id="A4.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\sigma c\sqrt{s}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>σ</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>c</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msqrt><mi>s</mi></msqrt></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\sigma c\sqrt{s}</annotation></semantics></math> to add to <math id="A4.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{\text{sim}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mtext>sim</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{\text{sim}}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The above privacy computation procedure is implemented in the open-source Private Evolution library.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          <a href="https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA/blob/main/pe/dp/gaussian.py" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/microsoft/DPSDA/blob/main/pe/dp/gaussian.py</a></span></span></span></p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T4" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A4.T4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 4</span>: </span><span id="A4.T4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Prompt used for constructing input prompts, as described in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 DP-RFT: Differentially-Private Reinforcement Finetuning ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</span></figcaption>
<table id="A4.T4.5" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="A4.T4.5.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A4.T4.5.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A4.T4.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:56.9pt;">
<span id="A4.T4.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.T4.5.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">Stage</span></span>
</span></td>
<td id="A4.T4.5.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_tt">
<span id="A4.T4.5.1.2.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:284.5pt;">
<span id="A4.T4.5.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.T4.5.1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">Prompt</span></span>

<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T6.5.2.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the quality of the response provided by an AI assistant to the user instruction displayed below. <span id="A4.T7.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A4.T7.5.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.T7.5.1.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:80%;">Prompts</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A4.T7.5.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A4.T7.5.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb ltx_border_t">
<span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:369.9pt;">
<span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"># Instruction </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the stylistic similarity of the responses provided by two AI assistants compared to the reference response. You should consider the elements such as use of words, style and tone. Do not consider the content match as the subject matter of the reference answer is different. Begin your evaluation by comparing both assistants’ answers with the reference answer. Identify the similarity and differences. Avoid any position biases and ensure that the order in which the responses were presented does not influence your decision. Do not allow the length of the responses to influence your evaluation. Do not favor certain names of the assistants. Be as objective as possible. After providing your explanation, output your final verdict by strictly following this format: [[A]] if assistant A is better, [[B]] if assistant B is better, and [[C]] for a tie.</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[Reference answer]</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">{reference_answer}</span><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;"> </span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[The Start of Assistant A’s Answer]</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">{assistant a answer}
<br class="ltx_break"></span><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[The End of Assistant A’s Answer]</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[The Start of Assistant B’s Answer]</span>
<br class="ltx_break"><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="font-size:80%;">{assistant b answer}
<br class="ltx_break"></span><span id="A4.T7.5.2.1.1.1.11" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">[The End of Assistant B’s Answer]</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>

<section id="A5.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.1.1 </span>Baseline details</h4>

<section id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Aug-PE</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the input prompt for  DP-RFT as <span id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">RANDOM_API</span> for  Aug-PE. We include samples of input prompts in <a href="#A4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 5</span></a>. For <span id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">VARIATION_API</span>, we use the <span id="A5.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fill-in-the-blank</span> following previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. We include the prompt in <a href="#A4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 8</span></a>. We set the max completion tokens the same as  DP-RFT and the blank probability to 0.6.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Choice of embedding model for <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The performance of DP-RFT correlates with how well <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> capture the similarity between the generated document and the private document. Will using more capable embedding model as <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math> induce more similar documents from the same base model? We perform an ablation study on the embedding model to understand how it impacts DP-RFT as well as Aug-PE. We experiment with using embedding models of three different scales from the GTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2023</a>)</cite> model families: gte-large (0.5B parameters), gte-1.5B and gte-7B. We conduct experiments on the PubMed dataset under the privacy setting with epsilon of {<math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, 4}.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results are reported in Table <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix F Ablation study ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. We observe that with more powerful embedding models, DP-RFT achieves better performance for both privacy budget. This suggests that DP-RFT has the potential to generate synthetic data with higher fidelity with the private data given an embedding model that can better capture the similarity with the private document. On the other hand, the improvement we observe for DP-RFT with bigger embedding model does not hold true for Aug-PE.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Choice of the language model for <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math>.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">How will the choice of <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math> influence the performance of  DP-RFT? We conduct an ablation study varying the backbone model <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{gen}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{gen}</annotation></semantics></math> while using the same embedding model (gte-1.5-B) as <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="R_{sim}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">R_{sim}</annotation></semantics></math>. We experiment with two model sizes from the QWEN family on the BBC article dataset: QWEN-2.5-3B-Instruct and QWEN-2.5-7B-Instruct and report downstream fine-tuning performance with epsilon of {<math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\infty</annotation></semantics></math>, 4}.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Results are in Table <a href="#A6.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix F Ablation study ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>. First, we see that the un-finetuned 7B model is able to generate better text compared to the 3B model, as reflected by improved performance of the QWEN baseline. Training 7B model with  DP-RFT also demonstrates better downstream performance compared to training 3B model. The trend with  Aug-PE is not as consistent, with performance improvement for <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=4" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=4</annotation></semantics></math> and performance degradation for <math id="A6.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon=\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon=\infty</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.T11" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A6.T11.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 11</span>: </span><span id="A6.T11.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Evaluation on downstream model performance using Qwen-2.5-3B-Instruct as the synthetic data generator. DP-RFT outperforms all baseline methods when there is a privacy constraint (<math id="A6.T11.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\neq\infty)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo fence="true" rspace="0em">OPEN</mo><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\neq\infty)</annotation></semantics></math> and with the same amount of data. The highest performance is <span id="A6.T11.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">bolded</span> while the second highest is <span id="A6.T11.6.2" class="ltx_text ltx_underline">underlined</span>. <section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Downstream evaluation with BERT<sub id="A7.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="A7.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">small</span></sub></h2>

<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For downstream evaluation of BERT<sub id="A7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">Small</sub>, we modify the bidirectional attention to causal attention. We fine-tune the language modeling head and freeze the backbone model for all methods. The model is trained with a batch size of 32, learning rate of <span id="A7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">3e-4</span> for 10 epochs. Following prior work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xie et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, we remove samples that are fewer than 50 tokens for downstream fine-tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report performance of fine-tuning BERT<sub id="A7.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="A7.p2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">small</span></sub> on the full set v.s. subset of private data, as well as generated synthetic text in <a href="#A6.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Choice of the language model for 𝑀_{𝑔⁢𝑒⁢𝑛}. ‣ Appendix F Ablation study ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 11</span></a>. We can see that DP-FT under-performs  DP-RFT when under privacy constraint (<math id="A7.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\neq\infty" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\neq\infty</annotation></semantics></math>) when training on the same amount of data across the four datsets. Scaling up the private data to full size enables better performance for DP-FT compared to  DP-RFT for PubMed and BBC. However, performance of DP-FT under privacy constraint still under-performs  DP-RFT for WildChat and QMSum, whose private data set size is significantly smaller.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A8" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix H </span>LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation</h2>

<figure id="A8.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2602.18633v1/dp_rft_vs_augpe_4panels.svg" id="A8.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:496/163;" width="496" height="163"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A8.F4.3" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="A8.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">LLM as a judge results for similarity measurement. We report both the win rate and the tie rate, included in the bracket. We compare samples generated by DP-RFT  against those generated by Aug-PE  under the same privacy budget (<math id="A8.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>ϵ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand <span id="A8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">how</span> a synthetic document is similar to a private document, we use <span id="A8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o</span> as an automatic evaluator to perform a pairwise similarity comparison of pairs of synthetic documents. Given a reference document, we prompt an LLM to choose the more similar synthetic document from a pair of data. As we are interested in the <span id="A8.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">style</span> of the generated documents, we randomly sample one private document as the reference answer to eliminate topical and semantic influence. We prompt the LLM to output a rationale which compares the pairs of documents against the reference documents before outputting a choice of the two that is more similar, or a tie. We choose the answer order at random to avoid positional bias of the judgment. For each dataset, we randomly sample 100 pairs of generation from  DP-RFT and  Aug-PE to conduct the evaluation.The exact prompt used are included in Table <a href="#A4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix D Privacy Analysis ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> in the Appendix.</p>
</div>
<section id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results</h5>

<div id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The results for all datasets are plotted in <a href="#A8.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 4</span></a>. Overall, it shows that  DP-RFT generates documents that are more similar to the private documents across all settings, consistent with the evaluation in §<a href="#S5.SS1" title="5.1 Downstream evaluation ‣ 5 Results ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5.1</span></a>. The rationale provided by the LM reveals similarity dimensions that are captured by  DP-RFT, such as use of direct quote for BBC articles, and use of simple and direct language for QMSum. We include example outputs from the LLM-as-a-judge in <a href="#A8.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Results ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 12</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.T12" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:80%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A8.T12.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Table 12</span>: </span><span id="A8.T12.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:113%;">Example output for similarity analysis. For the BBC article and PubMed, Answer B is from DP-RFT . For WildChat, Answer A is from Aug-PE .</span></figcaption>

<section id="A8.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">H.1 </span>Example text</h3>

<div id="A8.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We include example text from the private dataset, and generated text from DP-RFT  and Aug-PE  in Table <a href="#A8.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ H.1 Example text ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, <a href="#A8.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ H.1 Example text ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a>, <a href="#A8.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ H.1 Example text ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>, <a href="#A8.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ H.1 Example text ‣ Appendix H LLM-as-a-judge for similarity evaluation ‣ DP-RFT: Learning to Generate Synthetic Text via Differentially Private Reinforcement Fine-Tuning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A8.T13" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering" style="font-size:70%;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A8.T13.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Table 13</span>: </span><span id="A8.T13.7" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:129%;">Example private text and generated text for BBC article. We include example generation for <math id="A8.T13.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\epsilon\in\{\infty,1\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>ϵ</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">∞</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\epsilon\in\{\infty,1\}</annotation></semantics></math> for brevity.</span></figcaption>

<td id="A8.T14.8.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A8.T14.8.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">-</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A8.T14.8.2.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Private</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A8.T14.8.2.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:313.0pt;">
<span id="A8.T14.8.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Successful completion of the Intercollegiate Membership of the Royal Colleges of Surgeons (MRCS) examination is mandatory for surgical trainees entering higher specialist training in the United Kingdom. Despite its international reputation, and the value placed on the examination in surgical training, there has been little evidence of its predictive validity until recently. In this review, we present a summary of findings of four recent Intercollegiate studies assessing the predictive validity of the MRCS Part A (written) examination. Data from all four studies showed statistically significant positive correlations between the MRCS Part A and other written examinations taken by surgical trainees over the course of their education. The studies summarised in this review provide compelling evidence for the predictive validity of this gatekeeping examination. This review will be of interest to trainees, training institutions and the Royal Colleges given the value placed on the examination by surgical training programmes.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>

<td id="A8.T14.8.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">

<tr id="A8.T14.8.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A8.T14.8.4.1" class="ltx_td"></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.4.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left"><span id="A8.T14.8.4.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">DP-RFT</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.4.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top">
<span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:313.0pt;">
<span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">**Abstract**The use of placebo control in anesthesia care is a fundamental practice in clinical trials and anesthesia-related research to accurately assess the efficacy and safety of new therapeutic interventions. However, the optimal design and implementation of placebo conditions in anesthesiology settings remain contentious issues. This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and acceptability of different forms of placebo controls in adult patients undergoing elective orthopedic surgery under general anesthesia.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">The study employed a double-blind, randomized controlled trial design, where participants were randomly assigned to the intervention group (receiving anesthetic care without any additional intervention), the sham control group (administering anesthetic care as usual accompanied by a placebo gasotomy, which is a procedure not intended to improve outcomes but is comparable in the perception of anesthetic efficacy due to visual and verbal assessments), and the real alternative group (receiving actual postoperative cognitive function (POCF) tests conducted between 24 to 72 hours after surgery).</span></span>
<span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Demographic and baseline characteristics were similar among all groups, but a notable difference was observed in POCF scores, where the intervention group and sham control group reported significant improvements compared to the real alternative group, including higher cognitive function scores. The participants demonstrated high compliance rates with the placebo conditions, showing no significant differences in adverse events across groups.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.4.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">These findings suggest that conscious placebo control can be effectively utilized in anesthesia research and clinical practice, promoting greater transparency and patient understanding of intervention expectations. Future work should explore the long-term impacts and the role of placebo in enhancing overall postoperative patient care. Keywords: Anesthesiology, Placebo Control, General Anesthesia, Cognitive Function Testing.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A8.T14.8.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A8.T14.8.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A8.T14.8.5.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">1</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.5.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t"><span id="A8.T14.8.5.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Aug-PE</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.5.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_t">
<span id="A8.T14.8.5.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:313.0pt;">
<span id="A8.T14.8.5.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.5.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Title: Understanding Chromosome Segregation in Telomere Maintenance Cornerstone of Cellular Health Crucial during Division Where Accurate Segregation Plays a Pivotal Role Recent biogerontology has shed light on the regulatory mechanisms governing chromosome segregation, thereby ensuring fidelity in this critical process. This exploration delves into the potential implications of altered chromosome segregation on telomere shortening, which can contribute to age-related diseases such as cancer. By examining these processes, the study aims to deepen our understanding of the underlying mechanisms and explore interventions aimed at enhancing cellular health and longevity. Keywords: Chromosome Segregation, Telomere Maintenance, Aging, Biogerontology, Fidelity, Division</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A8.T14.8.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A8.T14.8.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_border_bb"></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="A8.T14.8.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">DP-RFT</span></td>
<td id="A8.T14.8.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:313.0pt;">
<span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Abstract: The study aimed to investigate the relationship between testicular function and the prevalence of genetic variants, specifically considering the impact of the tetraspanin 8 (TSPAN8) gene, in Indian subpopulation subjects. A quantitative genetic association study was conducted utilizing whole blood genomic DNA to identify single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and their correlation with testicular function parameters in 250 age-matched healthy males from the Indian mainland. Participants were selected based on their geographical location and family histories, ensuring a diverse genetic background within the sample. Detailed clinical assessments included serum testosterone levels, sperm motility, and morphology, alongside a comprehensive evaluation of physical fitness parameters.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Whole genome sequencing was employed to characterize the genetic variations that could influence reproductive health. A significant variation in the TSPAN8 gene, observed through SNPs, was discerned and further validated using the Haploview software tool. Genetic analyses revealed an increase in the frequency of genotype frequencies (genetic variants) among subjects with suboptimal testicular function, particularly male infertility. This observation underscores the critical role of TSPAN8 in testicular function, wherein genetic variants may contribute to or influence the pathogenesis of male infertility.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T14.8.6.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">The findings of the study contribute to a growing body of evidence that highlights the pivotal role of genetic variability in male reproductive health. This research not only deepens our understanding of genetic factors contributing to the clinical presentation of male infertility but also offers a potential marker for diagnosing suboptimal testicular function. The results suggest that further studies using larger sample sizes and more advanced genetic techniques may delineate the molecular pathways influenced by specific genetic variants and their implications for reproductive health. Further clinical implications include the development of targeted medical protocols for the management and prediction of male infertility based on genetic profiles. Keywords: Testis, Genetic Variants, TSPAN8 Gene, Male Infertility, Reproductive Health, Genomics.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>

<span id="A8.T16.8.2.3.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.2.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Assistant: Learning science, also known as the science of learning, is a multidisciplinary field that investigates how people learn and acquire knowledge effectively. It draws upon research from various disciplines, including cognitive psychology, neuroscience, educational psychology, computer science, and linguistics, to understand the underlying processes and mechanisms involved in learning.Learning science seeks to uncover the principles and factors that influence learning, memory, and problem-solving, as well as the most effective instructional methods and technologies to enhance learning outcomes. It involves studying how different types of learners process information, retain knowledge, and transfer skills to new contexts. Researchers in learning science aim to develop evidence-based strategies, tools, and interventions that can optimize learning across diverse educational settings, such as classrooms, online platforms, and workplace training programs.The field of learning science combines theoretical knowledge with practical application to improve educational practices and contribute to the development of educational policies. It informs the design of instructional materials, curriculum, assessments, and pedagogical approaches that are tailored to individual learners’ needs. Ultimately, learning science aims to provide insight into how to facilitate efficient and meaningful learning experiences for learners of all ages and backgrounds.</span></span>

<span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Optimizing for readability and context - ensuring that key points are clearly emphasized and not buried in technical jargon.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Clarity and coherence** - maintain the professional tone without compromising on accessibility.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Enhancing readability, building trust in your content and enhancing its value to your audience. Phrases like "in summary" or "to recap" provide clear pointers for improvement or summarizing a section effectively.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Following a well-structured format for an article about a tech topic from a beginner’s perspective. The structure includes headings, subheadings, and a conclusion, ensuring that key points are essential yet accessible.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.5.3.1.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Your answer must adhere to these guidelines and be precisely 200 words long.</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A8.T16.8.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A8.T16.8.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_border_bb"></td>
<td id="A8.T16.8.6.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">DP-RFT</span></td>
<td id="A8.T16.8.6.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_top ltx_border_bb">
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_top" style="width:313.0pt;">
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">User: Hi ChatGPT, could you help me visualize how photosynthesis works in a simple diagram?</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.2" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Assistant: User: Hi there! I think I’ve got a diagram that could help illustrate photosynthesis. Here’s a simple representation:</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">[Diagram: A green leaf with light shining on it, showing chloroplasts. Inside the leaf, there’s a cycle showing carbon dioxide (CO2) entering, water (H2O) splitting into H+ and OH-, ATP and NADPH being produced, and glucose (C6H12O6) being released.]</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.4" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">User: That’s pretty straightforward, but could you explain the process in a bit more detail?</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.5" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">Assistant: User: Of course! Let’s break it down step by step:</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.6" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">1. **Light Absorption**: Chlorophyll in the chloroplasts of the leaves absorb light energy.</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.7" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.7.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">2. **Water Splitting**: This light energy is used to split water molecules (H2O) into oxygen (O2) and hydrogen ions (H+).</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.8" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">3. **ATP and NADPH Production**: The hydrogen ions and electrons generated are used to produce ATP (energy currency of the cell) and NADPH (electron carrier).</span></span>
<span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.9" class="ltx_p"><span id="A8.T16.8.6.3.1.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:70%;">4. **Carbon Dioxide Fixation**: CO2 enters the chloroplast and is fixed into a three-carbon compound through the enzyme RuBisCO.[…],</span></span>
</span></td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
</figure>
</section>
